questions.q: Why does a scalar UDF called in a WHERE clause or SELECT list against many rows cause a performance problem, pre-SQL Server 2019?
options: The optimizer treats it as an opaque black box and executes it once per row, effectively an uncosted, invisible per-row loop
Scalar UDFs are not valid T-SQL and will raise a syntax error
Scalar UDFs can only return integer values
Scalar UDFs always require an explicit cursor to be declared alongside them
questions.explain: Because the optimizer can't see inside the function body to fold it into the query's plan, it falls back to calling it row-by-row, hidden from the visible plan operators.

questions.q: What is an inline table-valued function (iTVF)?
options: A function that returns a table via a single RETURN (SELECT ...) statement with no procedural body, letting the optimizer expand it into the calling query like a view
A scalar function that has been manually converted to run inside a WHILE loop
A function that can only be called from within a CURSOR declaration
A stored procedure that returns a scalar value
questions.explain: Because an iTVF is defined by a single query expression rather than a procedural body, SQL Server can substitute its definition directly into the surrounding query.

questions.q: What T-SQL operator is used to invoke a table-valued function per outer row within a set-based plan?
options: CROSS APPLY (or OUTER APPLY)
INNER JOIN only, never APPLY
PIVOT
MERGE
questions.explain: CROSS APPLY (or OUTER APPLY when the function may return no rows) invokes a table-valued function against each outer row as part of one set-based query.

questions.q: What is the recommended rewrite for a scalar UDF that computes a per-row total and is called against every row of a large table?
options: Convert its body into a single RETURN (SELECT ...) returning TABLE, and change call sites from a direct function call to CROSS APPLY
Wrap the existing scalar UDF call in a WHILE loop to make the row-by-row behavior explicit
Move the scalar UDF's logic into a trigger instead
There is no way to avoid the row-by-row cost; scalar UDFs must always be avoided entirely
questions.explain: Rewriting the function as an inline table-valued function and invoking it with CROSS APPLY lets the optimizer fold it into a normal set-based plan.

questions.q: Why does the lesson describe the scalar UDF performance problem as one the execution plan can hide?
options: The plan can look deceptively simple (e.g., a single scan) while the actual per-row function calls don't appear as separate, visible operators
Execution plans cannot be generated at all for queries that call scalar UDFs
SQL Server encrypts scalar UDF logic so it never appears in any diagnostic tool
Scalar UDF calls always show up as a distinct 'Scalar UDF' operator with an accurate cost, making them easy to spot
questions.explain: Because per-row scalar UDF calls aren't broken out as their own plan operators the way a join or lookup would be, the true per-row cost is easy to miss just from reading the plan.
